explanations.explanation: This neuron detects the use of “Let” (including “Let’s,” “Let us,” etc.) as the imperative-mood opener signaling a call-to-action, suggestion or invitation at the start of a sentence.

This feature detects parenthesized “aside” or metadata segments—i.e. tokens enclosed in () that carry structural labels or supplemental info (school/program names, dates, list indices, source tags, codes, color names, legal refs, etc.) rather than running prose.

This neuron appears to be flagging low-frequency, specialized subword tokens (uncommon words, proper names or technical terms), becoming strongly positive on rare or domain-specific fragments and negative on high-frequency function words.

This neuron is essentially a “first‐continuation” detector in BPE‐style tokenization: it lights up whenever you’re reading the second (or otherwise non‐initial) subword piece of a multi‐piece word—especially the unusual suffixes you find in proper names or specialized terms (e.g. “lem” in Flemish, “iz” in Leibniz, “over” in rollover, “omer” in Homer, etc.).
This feature detects explicit discourse-marker words—those adverbs or conjunctions (e.g. “though,” “because,” “way”) that signal contrast, cause, or transition in a sentence.

This neuron fires on discourse‐structuring and stance-taking cues—introductory/transition words and commentary verbs (e.g. “as you know,” “it is advisable,” “besides,” “in short,” “we’re pleased to announce,” “I wish,” “I thought,” “first,” etc.) that frame new points or express the speaker’s attitude.

This feature is simply a character-level n-gram detector that fires on common short letter sequences (2–4 letters) inside tokens (e.g. “il,” “ank,” “ick,” “urs,” “est,” etc.), irrespective of the word’s meaning.

This neuron is essentially a “root‐morpheme detector”: it lights up on the subword stems of content-heavy, often Latin/Greek-derived words (e.g. prote-, shop-, iod-, iat-, neurop-, cistern-, elig-, proceed-), i.e. the core morphemes that carry the main semantics of specialized terms.
This feature detects causal-consequence discourse markers—phrases like “As a result” that signal an outcome or effect.
This neuron fires on the main noun acting as the “title” or “label” in short headings or compound names—i.e. the head-noun of product names, section headings or category tags.

This neuron lights up on isolated alphanumeric “labels” or codes in technical/formal text—e.g. section or catalog numbers, IP-octets, model/version identifiers, product names (MAXON, Cinema 4D, Office 365), calibers (.22-250), DOI segments, etc.
This feature detects the structural “Q:” marker (and its punctuation) that labels the start of a question in a Q&A–style transcript.
This feature fires on subword pieces that form proper names—brands, product or model names, personal surnames, locations—i.e. it’s a general named‐entity detector.
This neuron is essentially a “number detector” — it lights up on tokens carrying discrete numeric information (years, dates, quantities, phone‐/route‐codes, measurements, etc.).

Here’s a concise characterization of each feature by the substring it fires on and the abstract concept it encodes:

• “aper” → the root “vap-/-vape” (vaper, vapor, vaporizer, vapegasm) – marks vaping-or‐vapor-related terms.  
• “edar” → the proper‐name element “Cedar” (parks, canyons, companies) – flags place or brand names beginning with Cedar.  
• “ver” → the suffix “-ver” in technical product names (converter, Perle Media Converters) – identifies device-oriented nomenclature.  
• “riv” → the root “arriv-” (arrivals) – signals words about arrival or coming.  
• “ider” → the noun “insider” (insider trading, insider perks) – highlights content about privileged/exclusive information or actors.  
• “vor” → the German preposition “vor” (“Recht vor …”) – picks out a common German function word indicating “before.”  
• “enn” → the name fragment in “Glenn” – detects that specific personal-name substring.  
• “urn” → the root “furn-” in “furniture” – tags furniture-related vocabulary.  
• “Prior” → the English adverb/preposition “prior” (prior to) – marks expressions of precedence.  
• “Di” → the name prefix “Di” (Di Lac, Diersen) – catches that element in personal surnames.  
• “oster” → the root “-oster” in words like “composter” – labels composting-oriented nouns.  
• “odeo” → the substring in “rodeo” – flags references to rodeo events or equipment.  
• “der” → the substring “der” in surnames like Derksen – isolates that common name-prefix.  
• “aper” (again) → the substring in “Naper” (Naperville) – marks that town-name element.

This feature is essentially a detector for short subword chunks—especially common consonant–vowel (and CV–consonant) sequences in English tokenization (e.g. “un,” “ou,” “ov,” “ur,” “urn,” “arch,” “aven,” etc.)—that frequently correspond to morpheme or syllable fragments.
This feature fires on proper‐noun place names (cities, states, regions, countries) – i.e. it detects mentions of geographic locations in text.
This neuron detects existential “there is/are/were” constructions used to enumerate or state the count/availability of items or entities (e.g. “There are 41…,” “There were 12…”).

This feature is a detector for the central morpheme of formal, content‐bearing words—especially Latin-derived roots and suffixes (e.g. port in im­port­ant/com­fort, fess in pro­fess­ion­als, res in re­search/re­served, pos in po­si­tion, ction in auc­tion, let in pal­ette)—which often appear as emphasized headings or key terms.

This neuron isn’t doing any deep semantics at all but rather flags very short BPE subword chunks – essentially one‐ to three-character fragments (single letters like “d” or “i,” a lone digit “3,” or tiny common prefixes like “Gib” or “Mo”) that result from the model’s byte-pair splits.
